# Effect Client Worker

NOTE: Startup and cleanup are handled by `mission-worker-base`. This skill
defines the work procedure.

## Required Skills and Tools

- Invoke `refactoring-playbook` before changing the retry interpreter.
- Invoke `codebase-design` when adding or changing the request Effect seam.
- Use mise for Node/pnpm commands.
- Use Vitest and Effect `TestClock` for deterministic timing.
- Attempt `entire graph search` once when required by repository guidance; if
  unavailable as documented, continue with focused source reads/search.

## Work Procedure

1. Read `mission.md`, `architecture.md`, `validation-contract.md`, `AGENTS.md`,
   `services.yaml`, `library/effect-v4.md`, and the assigned feature.
2. Inspect repository `AGENTS.md`, relevant CONTRIBUTING/test-lane guidance,
   current branch status, and only the focused client/Worker symbols needed.
3. Identify the smallest behavior-preserving seam for the assigned feature.
   Preserve public Promise and `HevyHttpError` contracts and all package
   boundaries.
4. Write focused failing tests first. Tests must exercise public behavior or
   the internal production request Effect seam, never a parallel test-only
   retry implementation.
5. Run the focused test and record the expected red failure.
6. Implement the smallest complete Effect v4 change:
   - typed internal error channels with sufficient metadata;
   - request-local schedule state;
   - Effect Clock/sleep for default timing;
   - custom Promise sleep adaptation;
   - exactly-once resource finalizers;
   - one outer runtime boundary.
7. Run focused tests until green. Add concurrency and late-settlement checks
   where the feature touches shared state, cancellation, observers, or
   resources.
8. Run `mise exec -- pnpm run test:unit` and
   `mise exec -- pnpm run check:types`.
9. If runtime/bundle paths changed, run `test:worker`, `test:worker-http`, and
   `worker:dry-run`.
10. Run formatting/lint checks for changed files. Review the complete diff for
    generated files, Node built-ins, broad types/casts, duplicated policy,
    secrets, and unrelated changes.
11. Add/update the required non-empty Changeset before committing. Use a
    Conventional Commit and include the required Factory co-author. Do not
    push.
12. Return a thorough handoff with exact commands, test identifiers, commit,
    remaining work, and discovered issues.

**Tools:** Use mise for all Node/pnpm commands. Use named repository test lanes.

migration and `codebase-design` when defining or changing the interpreter
seam. Always follow `mission-worker-base` startup/cleanup.

**Dependencies:** Use the existing `effect@4.0.0-rc.112`. Do not add or
substitute an Effect version or retry library.

**Other requirements:**

- Strict red-green-refactor TDD.
- Preserve Promise-facing APIs and `HevyHttpError` projections.
- Keep exactly one outer Effect runtime boundary per logical request.

- A caller-supplied explicit deadline is authoritative and terminal.

  consume scheduled backoff.

- `mise exec -- pnpm run test:unit`

# Effect v4 Retry Patterns

Worker-facing Effect v4 RC API constraints and approved patterns.

---

- Import `TestClock` from `effect/testing`.
- `Effect.async` does not exist in this version; the callback primitive is
  `Effect.callback`.
- `Effect.tryPromise` accepts an interruption signal and must use an explicit
  catch mapping.
- Use `Schedule.toStep` for the interpreter because it must inspect/cap delay,
  control wait observations, support custom sleep, and classify sleep failure.
- `Schedule.toStepWithSleep` is unsuitable for this lifecycle because it hides
  the sleep seam.
- Schedule steps are stateful. Construct one inside every logical request.
- Schedule completion uses `Pull`/`Cause.Done`; avoid stepping beyond the known
  retry budget or handle completion explicitly.
- Use `Clock.currentTimeMillis` and `Effect.sleep` for default backoff.
- Use `Effect.ensuring` or scoped finalization for cleanup on success, typed
  failure, defect, and interruption.
- Do not pass the caller AbortSignal directly to `Effect.runPromise` unless
  Cause-level interruption is projected back to the established public
  `HevyHttpError`.
- Build one request Effect and call `Effect.runPromise` once at the Promise
  adapter boundary. Do not nest runtime executions.

description: Migrate the Hevy client retry lifecycle to Effect v4 while preserving public behavior.
---

# Effect Client Worker

NOTE: Startup and cleanup are handled by `mission-worker-base`. This skill
defines the work procedure.

## Required Skills and Tools

- Invoke `refactoring-playbook` before changing the retry interpreter.
- Invoke `codebase-design` when adding or changing the request Effect seam.
- Use mise for Node/pnpm commands.
- Use Vitest and Effect `TestClock` for deterministic timing.
- Attempt `entire graph search` once when required by repository guidance; if
  unavailable as documented, continue with focused source reads/search.

## Work Procedure

1. Read `mission.md`, `architecture.md`, `validation-contract.md`, `AGENTS.md`,
   `services.yaml`, `library/effect-v4.md`, and the assigned feature.
2. Inspect repository `AGENTS.md`, relevant CONTRIBUTING/test-lane guidance,
   current branch status, and only the focused client/Worker symbols needed.
3. Identify the smallest behavior-preserving seam for the assigned feature.
   Preserve public Promise and `HevyHttpError` contracts and all package
   boundaries.
4. Write focused failing tests first. Tests must exercise public behavior or
   the internal production request Effect seam, never a parallel test-only
   retry implementation.
5. Run the focused test and record the expected red failure.
6. Implement the smallest complete Effect v4 change:
   - typed internal error channels with sufficient metadata;
   - request-local schedule state;
   - Effect Clock/sleep for default timing;
   - custom Promise sleep adaptation;
   - exactly-once resource finalizers;
   - one outer runtime boundary.
7. Run focused tests until green. Add concurrency and late-settlement checks
   where the feature touches shared state, cancellation, observers, or
   resources.
8. Run `mise exec -- pnpm run test:unit` and
   `mise exec -- pnpm run check:types`.
9. If runtime/bundle paths changed, run `test:worker`, `test:worker-http`, and
   `worker:dry-run`.
10. Run formatting/lint checks for changed files. Review the complete diff for
    generated files, Node built-ins, broad types/casts, duplicated policy,
    secrets, and unrelated changes.
11. Add/update the required non-empty Changeset before committing. Use a
    Conventional Commit and include the required Factory co-author. Do not
    push.
12. When the assigned feature is complete and the named checks are green, call
    `end_feature_run` in the same turn. The runner cannot record the feature
    without that call. Include successState, salientSummary, whatWasImplemented,
    discoveredIssues, whatWasLeftUndone, exact commands with exit codes, commitId,
    and repoPath. If verification did not run, set successState to partial or
    failure and returnToOrchestrator=true — never claim success from type
    inspection or invented files.
13. Do not invent modules, commits, or test results. Work only in
    `/root/hevy-mcp-effect-retry-interpreter` on `feat/effect-retry-interpreter`.
    If a previous handoff described work that is not present in this worktree,
    ignore it and implement the assigned feature from the current files.

## Example Handoff

## When to Return to Orchestrator

- Preserving a current behavior conflicts with the approved explicit-deadline
  correction or architecture.
- An Effect v4 API differs from `library/effect-v4.md` in a way that changes the
  design.
- A fix requires public API, package topology, generated output, Node policy, or
  live-service changes.
- Deterministic cancellation/deadline arbitration cannot be expressed without
  adding a new test seam that needs architectural approval.
- Existing unrelated failures prevent verifying the assigned behavior.

# Mission Worker Guidance

## Mission Boundaries (NEVER VIOLATE)

**Repository:** `/root/hevy-mcp-effect-retry-interpreter`

**Branch:** `feat/effect-retry-interpreter`, stacked from PR #1104 commit
`1073abb`. Do not rebase onto main during the mission.

**Ports and services:** No long-running service or claimed port is required.
Do not start persistent watch, dev-server, or browser processes.

**External services:** Deterministic mocked validation only. Do not call the
live Hevy API and do not require, read, print, or persist `HEVY_API_KEY`.

**Off-limits:**

- `packages/hevy-client/src/generated/` must not be edited.
- `/root/hevy-mcp` untracked `.pi-subagents/` and `.worktrees/` are user state.
- PR #1104 and remote branches must not be modified or pushed.
- Do not change public Node compatibility, package topology, or unrelated
  adapters.

If the feature cannot be completed inside these boundaries, return to the
orchestrator.

## Mission Directives

**Tools:** Use mise for all Node/pnpm commands. Use named repository test lanes.
Attempt the documented `entire graph` search first for locate/change work, but
the CLI is known unavailable; after one failed probe, use focused repository
search and reads rather than retrying.

**Skills:** Invoke and follow `refactoring-playbook` for behavior-preserving
migration and `codebase-design` when defining or changing the interpreter
seam. Always follow `mission-worker-base` startup/cleanup. When the assigned
feature is complete and checks are green, call `end_feature_run` in the same
turn with the handoff. Never end a turn after writing code without that call.

**Dependencies:** Use the existing `effect@4.0.0-rc.112`. Do not add or
substitute an Effect version or retry library.

**Other requirements:**

- Strict red-green-refactor TDD.
- Preserve Promise-facing APIs and `HevyHttpError` projections.
- Keep exactly one outer Effect runtime boundary per logical request.
- Create schedule state per request, never per client.
- Default backoff uses Effect Clock/sleep; custom Promise sleep remains
  compatible.
- Preserve existing endpoint, safety, commit-state, retry, and diagnostics
  policies instead of creating parallel policy logic.
- No `any`, broad `unknown` helper contracts, manual casts, or Node built-ins in
  runtime-neutral packages.
- Observer callbacks are best-effort and may not duplicate dispatch or
  completion.
- Every opened attempt, signal, body, timer, fiber, and wait scope must finalize
  exactly once.
- Keep hooks enabled and use Conventional Commits with the Factory co-author.
- Before each commit, add the required non-empty Changeset when the diff
  triggers release coverage.

## Coding and Architecture Conventions

- Keep the Kubb client Promise signature unchanged.
- Internal tagged failures must carry all metadata required for exact public
  projection; do not replace `HevyHttpError` with a lossy Effect error class.
- Prefer one deep request-interpreter module/seam over scattered Effect
  wrappers.
- Keep retry eligibility pure. The schedule owns retry index and delay only.
- Use Effect finalizers rather than parallel manual cleanup paths.
- A caller-supplied explicit deadline is authoritative and terminal.
- The immediate implicit read deadline retry does not sleep, open a wait, or
  consume scheduled backoff.

## Testing & Validation Guidance

Workers run the narrowest tests first, then:

- `mise exec -- pnpm run test:unit`
- `mise exec -- pnpm run check:types`
- Runtime compatibility changes also run `test:worker`, `test:worker-http`, and
  `worker:dry-run`.

The milestone validator runs commands from `services.yaml` sequentially.
Maximum concurrent validators is 1 due to current CPU saturation.

Expected stderr from negative-path Worker tests is not a failure when the
command exits zero. Live credential-gated lanes are out of scope.

# User Testing

Validation surfaces, prerequisites, and concurrency guidance.

## Validation Surface

The user-visible surface is the native Promise Hevy client API and its Worker
adapter projection. Use deterministic Vitest client calls, mocked HTTP, local
Wrangler/Workerd integration, package/boundary checks, and build artifacts.
Browser and TUI tools do not apply.

## Validation Prerequisites

- Pinned mise/Node/pnpm toolchain verified.
- Effect v4, Vitest, Nx, Wrangler, and Workerd imports/commands verified.
- Focused tests, unit, Worker, Worker HTTP, Worker dry-run, and type checks
  passed with `HEVY_API_KEY` explicitly unset.
- No allowlist, external account, port, seed data, or live credential is needed.
- TestClock controls Effect time only; actual client tests must execute the
  internal production request Effect under the TestClock layer.

## Validation Concurrency

Maximum concurrent validators: **1**.

Readiness measurements: 8 CPU cores, approximately 13 GiB available memory,
and load average above the core count. Memory could support more, but
Vitest/Nx/Workerd fan out internally and parallel validators would oversubscribe
CPU. Run validation commands sequentially.

## Evidence

Collect terminal command/exit status, exact passing test identifiers, attempt
and callback event arrays, public error field snapshots, TestClock boundaries,
Worker HTTP envelopes, and bundle/boundary/check output as required by
`validation-contract.md`.

### VAL-COMPAT-001: Promise-facing client contract remains unchanged
Every curated `createHevyClient` operation returns a native Promise, successful calls resolve to the existing decoded values, and terminal calls reject with `HevyHttpError` carrying the existing camelCase and snake_case execution metadata. No Effect `Cause`, `Exit`, fiber, service, or mission-internal tagged failure is observable, and all 22 generated-wrapper operations still dispatch exactly once when retries are disabled.
Tool: `mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts` + exit 0), assertions(native Promise results, 22 dispatches, `instanceof HevyHttpError`, stable code/status/phase/outcome/commit-state/safety aliases, no Effect values)

### VAL-COMPAT-002: Request-local retry state is independent
Two sequential requests and two concurrently pending requests made through one client each begin at retry index zero, receive their full configured retry budget, and independently produce the same first and second schedule delays. Advancing, exhausting, cancelling, or completing one request must not alter another request's attempt count, retry index, delay, or result.
Tool: `mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts` + exit 0), assertions(per-request retry indexes `[0,1,2]`, independent delays, exact fetch counts, independent fulfilled/rejected results)

### VAL-COMPAT-003: Default backoff uses the Effect test clock
The actual `createHevyClient` default-sleep path remains pending before its scheduled delay, performs no early second fetch, and performs the next attempt only after `TestClock` advances through the computed delay. The request then resolves through the public Promise API without real-time sleeping.
Tool: `mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts packages/hevy-client/src/retry-schedule.test.ts`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts packages/hevy-client/src/retry-schedule.test.ts` + exit 0), assertions(one fetch before clock adjustment, two fetches after adjustment, resolved public value, no wall-clock timer dependency)

### VAL-COMPAT-004: Cloudflare Workerd executes the migrated client
The Worker test lane starts the configured module in the Cloudflare Vitest Workerd pool and successfully serves representative Worker routes without Node globals or built-ins. The production Worker bundle dry-run also completes and passes the repository bundle inspection with Effect and the client interpreter included.
Tool: `mise exec -- pnpm run test:worker && mise exec -- pnpm run worker:dry-run`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- pnpm run test:worker && mise exec -- pnpm run worker:dry-run` + both commands exit 0), assertions(Workerd route responses, OAuth challenge/metadata, Wrangler bundle created, bundle inspection passed)

### VAL-COMPAT-005: Worker HTTP preserves retry exhaustion projection
Through the real local Wrangler/Workerd HTTP path, an invalid upstream credential produces one upstream 401 and an HTTP 401 bearer challenge, while a transient upstream 503 produces exactly three upstream attempts for the configured two retries and then HTTP 502. The 502 body contains the existing sanitized `HevyHttpError` projection, including status 503, terminal outcome, phase, operation safety, commit state, and `safe_to_retry: false`, and contains neither credentials nor Effect internals.
Tool: `mise exec -- pnpm run test:worker-http`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- pnpm run test:worker-http` + exit 0), assertions(upstream key sequence, exact attempt counts 1 and 3, HTTP statuses 401 and 502, bearer challenge, projected error fields, secret/Internal-Effect absence)

### VAL-COMPAT-006: Runtime-neutral package boundaries hold
`hevy-client`, `operations`, and `core` import no Node built-ins, Cloudflare-only modules, forbidden observability modules, or escaping relative paths; `worker` imports no Node built-ins; and dependency direction remains the topology-approved client-to-operations-to-core-to-adapter graph. No new non-literal dynamic import appears where topology forbids it.
Tool: `mise exec -- pnpm run check:boundaries`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- pnpm run check:boundaries` + exit 0), assertions(package-boundary checker passed, dependency-cruiser passed, no forbidden runtime/import edge)

### VAL-COMPAT-007: Generated client output is stable
Regenerating from the normalized checked-in OpenAPI document and Kubb configuration in an isolated temporary tree yields a byte-for-byte match with `packages/hevy-client/src/generated/`, creates no repository-root `src/` tree, and leaves curated type/schema barrels valid. The retry migration introduces no tracked generated-file changes.
Tool: `mise exec -- pnpm run check:generated`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- pnpm run check:generated` + exit 0 and “Generated client is up to date”), assertions(no missing/unexpected/different generated files, no forbidden root source, curated barrels type-check, generated git diff empty)

### VAL-COMPAT-008: Changeset covers the complete shipped cascade
The branch contains a non-empty release Changeset naming `@hevy-mcp/hevy-client` and every transitive shipped consumer required by repository topology: `@hevy-mcp/operations`, `@hevy-mcp/core`, `hevy-mcp`, `@hevy-mcp/worker`, and `@chrisdoc/hevy-cli`, each with at least a patch bump. It contains no empty companion Changeset and no unrelated package release.
Tool: `mise exec -- pnpm run check:changeset`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- pnpm run check:changeset` + exit 0), assertions(changeset status passed, six-package cascade present, all bumps non-empty, no missing or unrelated release)

### VAL-CROSS-001: Retry observations balance attempts and waits
A transient read failure followed by success produces exactly two fetches, request starts at retry counts zero and one, exactly one completion per attempt in order (`retryable_failure`, then `success`), and exactly one retry-wait scope that starts and finishes before attempt one begins. Fetch dispatch and response consumption remain inside the request observation scope, and observer callbacks receive only bounded metadata.
Tool: `mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts` + exit 0), assertions(ordered attempt/wait events, two starts, two finishes, one balanced wait, two fetches, bounded observation payloads)

### VAL-CROSS-002: Cancellation finalizes retry wait without redispatch
When caller cancellation wins during either custom or default retry backoff, the Promise rejects once with a public cancellation `HevyHttpError` in phase `backoff` and `safe_to_retry: false`; no later attempt starts even if custom sleep subsequently resolves. The active retry-wait scope finishes exactly once, completed attempt observations are not duplicated, and default-path timers and abort listeners are cleaned up.
Tool: `mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts` + exit 0), assertions(one fetch, one rejection, balanced attempt/wait finishes, no post-cancel start, zero timers, no duplicate listener callback)

### VAL-CROSS-003: Explicit deadlines create no impossible retry
A read with an authoritative caller deadline that expires during its first attempt performs one fetch and rejects with `HEVY_DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, `deadline_exceeded`, and the correct phase. It emits one attempt completion and no retry log, retry-wait start, retry-wait finish, sleep call, or second attempt.
Tool: `mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts` + exit 0), assertions(one fetch, one deadline error, one attempt completion, zero retry logs, zero waits/sleeps, zero leaked timers/listeners)

### VAL-CROSS-004: Implicit read deadline retry uses a fresh budget
For an implicit timeout on a safe read, the client performs exactly one immediate fresh-budget retry, does not consume or sleep on the normal schedule for that transition, and can resolve from the second attempt. If the second attempt also times out, it rejects with the public deadline error; in both cases each started attempt completes exactly once and no retry-wait scope is opened for the immediate transition.
Tool: `mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts` + exit 0), assertions(two fetches, zero scheduled sleeps/waits, retry counts zero and one, two balanced completions, success-or-deadline public projection)

### VAL-CROSS-005: Concurrent cancellation is request-local
When two retrying reads share one client and only one caller signal is aborted, the cancelled request rejects with the cancellation projection and performs no further fetch, while the other request retains its own retry schedule, completes all expected attempts, and resolves. Attempt and retry-wait observations for both requests remain individually balanced and correlation-safe.
Tool: `mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts` + exit 0), assertions(one local cancellation, unaffected peer success, independent exact fetch counts/indexes/delays, balanced per-request observations)

### VAL-CROSS-006: Backoff failures remain adapter-safe
If the Promise-based custom sleep hook rejects after a retryable response, the client starts no second fetch and rejects with the established public backoff `HevyHttpError` rather than an Effect defect or raw sleep exception. Passing that error through the Worker adapter yields the existing sanitized HTTP status and error envelope, with phase `backoff`, `safe_to_retry: false`, and no exception text, cause, credential, or Effect internals.
Tool: `mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts packages/worker/src/worker.test.ts`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts packages/worker/src/worker.test.ts` + exit 0), assertions(one fetch, public backoff error, stable Worker status/envelope, bounded metadata, secret/raw-cause/Internal-Effect absence)

### VAL-CROSS-007: Worker cancellation and deadline projections preserve lifecycle outcomes
A cancelled Worker request forwards the request signal to client validation, performs no retry after abort, and returns HTTP 499 with outcome `cancelled`; a client deadline outcome returns HTTP 504 with outcome `deadline_exceeded`. Both envelopes preserve phase, commit state, and `safe_to_retry: false`, and neither is rewritten as generic terminal failure or retry exhaustion.
Tool: `mise exec -- vitest run packages/worker/src/worker.test.ts`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- vitest run packages/worker/src/worker.test.ts` + exit 0), assertions(signal identity, no extra client call, statuses 499/504, cancellation/deadline outcomes, stable metadata, no generic terminal rewrite)

### VAL-CROSS-008: Retry exhaustion remains coherent across client and Worker HTTP
A 503 sequence exhausts exactly the configured client retry budget, completes each attempt observation once, completes exactly one fewer retry-wait scopes than attempts, and exposes a terminal `HEVY_RETRY_EXHAUSTED` error with `safe_to_retry: false`. The real Worker HTTP adapter converts that same exhausted upstream condition to one HTTP 502 response after exactly three upstream requests, without initiating an adapter-level retry loop.
Tool: `mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts && mise exec -- pnpm run test:worker-http`
Evidence: terminal(`mise exec -- vitest run packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts && mise exec -- pnpm run test:worker-http` + both commands exit 0), assertions(exact attempts/completions/waits, retry-exhausted client code, three upstream requests, one HTTP response, status 502, no duplicate adapter retries)

# Complete Effect Retry Interpreter

## Plan Overview

Complete the Hevy client retry migration begun in PR #1104 by moving the entire retry execution lifecycle into one Effect v4 program per logical request. The work will land on `feat/effect-retry-interpreter`, stacked from commit `1073abb` at the head of #1104.

The migration must preserve the current Promise-facing public API and runtime behavior while eliminating shared schedule state, making default backoff and resource cleanup Effect-native, and correcting the caller-deadline retry-wait lifecycle defect approved during planning.

## Expected Functionality

### Milestone: Effect Retry Interpreter

1. **Characterize independent retry state and lifecycle behavior**
   - Add regression coverage proving sequential and concurrent operations on one client have independent retry budgets, schedule attempt indexes, cancellation, and observations.
   - Cover retry-wait finalization, cancellation/deadline races, and exact attempt/completion counts.

2. **Build Effect-native attempt and backoff primitives**
   - Represent attempt failures and retry transitions with internal typed errors/unions.
   - Bridge fetch, response consumption, and optional custom sleep through Effect v4 primitives.
   - Use `Effect.ensuring` for attempt listeners, retry-wait scopes, and execution-signal cleanup.
   - Use Effect `Clock`/`Effect.sleep` for default backoff so the actual client path is controllable with `TestClock`.

3. **Integrate the per-request retry interpreter**
   - Replace the imperative retry loop and nested runtime crossings with one recursive Effect program and one `Effect.runPromise` boundary.
   - Instantiate `Schedule.toStep(createRetrySchedule(...))` separately for every logical request.
   - Preserve retry limits, exponential backoff/jitter, `Retry-After`, absolute and per-attempt deadlines, the single fresh-budget read deadline retry, method safety, commit-state metadata, observations, diagnostics, and exhaustion behavior.
   - Correct the explicit caller-deadline path so it does not open/log an impossible retry or leak an unfinished retry-wait scope.
   - Verify Node and Cloudflare Worker compatibility and review affected README guidance for accuracy.

## Architecture

The Kubb client remains the Promise-based adapter boundary. Inside each request, a single Effect program owns the request lifecycle:

1. Acquire the combined caller/deadline execution signal.
2. Create a request-local retry schedule step.
3. Execute one typed attempt Effect.
4. Classify failure through the existing pure safety and endpoint policies.
5. Return terminal errors immediately, refresh the deadline for the one special read retry, or advance the schedule and execute an interruptible backoff Effect.
6. Recurse with updated retry state.
7. Finalize signals, listeners, and observation scopes on success, failure, defect, or interruption.
8. Convert the final Effect to the existing Promise contract exactly once.

The schedule owns timing and retry index only. Existing client policy remains authoritative for whether retrying is safe. Public `HevyHttpError` remains the externally observable error contract; internal Effect failures must never leak as Effect causes.

Package direction remains `hevy-client -> operations -> core -> adapters`. No Node built-ins enter runtime-neutral packages, and generated client files remain untouched.

### Navigation\
\
[Permalink: Navigation](https://github.com/github/gh-stack#navigation)\
\
Move between branches in the current stack without having to remember branch names.\
\
```\
gh stack up [n]      # Move up n branches (default 1)\
gh stack down [n]    # Move down n branches (default 1)\
gh stack top         # Jump to the top of the stack\
gh stack bottom      # Jump to the bottom of the stack\
gh stack trunk       # Jump to the trunk branch\
gh stack switch      # Interactively pick a branch to switch to\
```\
\
Navigation commands clamp to the bounds of the stack — moving up from the top or down from the bottom is a no-op with a message. If you're on the trunk branch, `up` moves to the first stack branch.\
\
**Examples:**\
\
```\
gh stack up          # move up one layer\
gh stack up 3        # move up three layers\
gh stack down\
gh stack top\
gh stack bottom\
gh stack trunk       # jump to the trunk branch (e.g., main)\
gh stack switch      # shows an interactive picker\
```\
\
### `gh stack feedback`\
\
[Permalink: gh stack feedback](https://github.com/github/gh-stack#gh-stack-feedback)\
\
Share feedback about gh-stack.\
\
```\
gh stack feedback [title]\
```\
\
Opens a GitHub Discussion in the [gh-stack repository](https://github.com/github/gh-stack) to submit feedback. Optionally provide a title for the discussion post.\
\
**Examples:**\
\
```\
gh stack feedback\
gh stack feedback "Support for reordering branches"\
```\
\
### `gh stack alias`\
\
[Permalink: gh stack alias](https://github.com/github/gh-stack#gh-stack-alias)\
\
Create a short command alias so you can type less.\
\
```\
gh stack alias [flags] [name]\
```\
\
Installs a small wrapper script into `~/.local/bin/` that forwards all arguments to `gh stack`. The default alias name is `gs`, but you can choose any name by passing it as an argument. After setup, you can run `gs push` instead of `gh stack push`.\
\
On Windows, automatic alias creation is not supported — the command prints manual instructions for creating a batch file or PowerShell function.\
\
| Flag | Description |\
| --- | --- |\
| `--remove` | Remove a previously created alias |\
\
**Examples:**\
\
```\
# Create the default alias (gs)\
gh stack alias\
#    → now "gs push", "gs view", etc. all work\
\
# Create a custom alias\
gh stack alias gst\
\
# Remove an alias\
gh stack alias --remove\
gh stack alias gst --remove\
```\
\
## Typical workflow\
\
[Permalink: Typical workflow](https://github.com/github/gh-stack#typical-workflow)\
\
```\
# 1. Start a stack (creates and checks out the first branch)\
gh stack init\
\
# 2. Work on the first layer\
#    ... write code, make commits ...\
\
# 3. Add the next layer\
gh stack add api-routes\
#    ... write code, make commits ...\
\
# 4. Push everything and create Stacked PRs\
gh stack submit\
\
# 5. Reviewer requests changes on the first PR\
gh stack bottom\
#    ... make changes, commit ...\
\
# 6. Rebase the rest of the stack on top of your fix\
gh stack rebase\
\
# 7. Push the updated branches\
gh stack push\
\
# 8. When the first PR is merged, sync the stack\
gh stack sync\
# → prompts to prune merged branches (or use --prune to prune automatically and avoid the prompt)\
```\
\
## Abbreviated workflow\
\
[Permalink: Abbreviated workflow](https://github.com/github/gh-stack#abbreviated-workflow)\
\
If you want to minimize keystrokes, use the `-Am` flags to fold staging, committing, and branch creation into a single command. When you don't pass a branch name, one is auto-generated from the commit message in date+slug format (e.g., `03-24-auth_middleware`).\
\
When a branch has no commits yet (e.g., right after `init`), `add -Am` stages and commits directly on that branch instead of creating a new one. Once a branch has commits, `add -Am` creates a new branch, checks it out, and commits there.\
\
```\
# 1. Start a stack\
gh stack init auth\
#    → creates auth and checks it out\
\
# 2. Write code for the first layer\
#    ... write code ...\
\
# 3. Stage and commit on the current branch\
gh stack add -Am "Auth middleware"\
#    → auth has no commits yet, so the commit lands here\
#      (no new branch is created)\
\
# 4. Write code for the next layer\
#    ... write code ...\
\
# 5. Create the next branch and commit\
gh stack add -Am "API routes"\
#    → auth already has commits, so a new branch is created from the\
#      commit message, checked out, and the commit lands there\
\
# 6. Keep going\
#    ... write code ...\
\
gh stack add -Am "Frontend components"\
#    → creates another branch and commits there\
\
# 7. Push everything and create PRs\
gh stack submit\
```\
\
Compared to the typical workflow, there's no need to name branches, run `git add`, or run `git commit` separately. Each `gh stack add -Am "..."` does it all. Pass an explicit branch name any time you want to control it: `gh stack add -Am "API routes" api-routes`.\
\
## Terminal theme\
\
[Permalink: Terminal theme](https://github.com/github/gh-stack#terminal-theme)\
\
The interactive screens (`submit`, `modify`, and `view`) and all colored command output (status messages, prompts) automatically adapt their colors to your terminal's background, so they're readable on both dark and light themes. The background is detected from the terminal; if a terminal doesn't report it (some SSH or `tmux` setups), the dark palette is used.\
\
Set `GH_STACK_THEME` to force a palette if detection is wrong:\
\
| Value | Behavior |\
| --- | --- |\
| `auto` (default) | Detect from the terminal background |\
| `light` | Force the light palette |\
| `dark` | Force the dark palette |\
\
```\
# Force the light palette\
export GH_STACK_THEME=light && gh stack view\
```\
\
## Exit codes\
\
[Permalink: Exit codes](https://github.com/github/gh-stack#exit-codes)\
\
| Code | Meaning |\
| --- | --- |\
| 0 | Success |\
| 1 | Generic error |\
| 2 | Not in a stack / stack not found |\
| 3 | Rebase conflict |\
| 4 | GitHub API failure |\
| 5 | Invalid arguments or flags |\
| 6 | Disambiguation required (branch belongs to multiple stacks) |\
| 7 | Rebase already in progress |\
| 8 | Stack is locked by another process |\

# Stacked pull requests CLI commands

Find every command, flag, and exit code for the `gh stack` extension in GitHub CLI.

Copy as Markdown

## In this article

Note

This feature is in public preview and subject to change.

The `gh stack` extension for GitHub CLI creates and manages stacks of pull requests from your local repository. For an introduction to stacks, see [Stacked pull requests](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-pull-requests).

## [Installation](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#installation)

```shell
gh extension install github/gh-stack
```

The extension requires GitHub CLI (`gh`) version 2.0 or later.

Note

The `gh stack` extension uses your GitHub CLI authentication. If you have not authenticated yet, run `gh auth login`.

## [Command summary](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#command-summary)

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| [`gh stack init`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-init) | Initialize a new stack in the current repository. |
| [`gh stack add`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-add) | Add a new branch on top of the current stack. |
| [`gh stack view`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-view) | View the current stack. |
| [`gh stack checkout`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-checkout) | Check out a stack by stack number, pull request number, pull request URL, or branch name. |
| [`gh stack modify`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-modify) | Interactively restructure the current stack. |
| [`gh stack unstack`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-unstack) | Remove a stack from local tracking and unstack it on GitHub. |
| [`gh stack submit`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-submit) | Push all branches, then create or update pull requests and the stack on GitHub. |
| [`gh stack sync`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-sync) | Fetch, rebase, push, and sync pull request state in a single command. |
| [`gh stack rebase`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-rebase) | Pull from the remote and run a cascading rebase across the stack. |
| [`gh stack push`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-push) | Push the active branches in the current stack to the remote. |
| [`gh stack link`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-link) | Link pull requests into a stack on GitHub without local tracking. |
| [`gh stack merge`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-merge) | Merge one or more stacked pull requests at once. |
| [`gh stack switch`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-switch) | Interactively switch to another branch in the stack. |
| [`gh stack up`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-up) | Move up toward the top of the stack, away from the trunk. |
| [`gh stack down`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-down) | Move down toward the bottom of the stack, toward the trunk. |
| [`gh stack top`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-top) | Jump to the top of the stack. |
| [`gh stack bottom`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-bottom) | Jump to the bottom of the stack. |
| [`gh stack trunk`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-trunk) | Jump to the trunk branch. |
| [`gh stack alias`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-alias) | Create a short command alias so you can type less. |
| [`gh stack feedback`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#gh-stack-feedback) | Share feedback about the `gh stack` extension. |

## [Stack management](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#stack-management)

### [`gh stack init`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-init)

Initialize a new stack in the current repository.

```shell
gh stack init [flags] [branches...]
```

Initializes a new stack locally. In interactive mode (no arguments), the command prompts for a branch name and offers to use the current branch as the first layer.

When you provide explicit branch names, existing branches are adopted automatically and any missing branches are created. The trunk defaults to the repository's default branch unless you override it with `--base`.

The command enables `git rerere` automatically, so that conflict resolutions are remembered across rebases.

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-b, --base <branch>` | Trunk branch for the stack (defaults to the repository's default branch) |

**Examples:**

```shell
# Interactive — prompts for branch names
gh stack init

# Non-interactive — specify first branch upfront
gh stack init feature-auth

# Use a different trunk branch
gh stack init --base develop feature-auth

# Adopt or create multiple branches at once
gh stack init feature-auth feature-api feature-ui
```

### [`gh stack add`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-add)

Add a new branch on top of the current stack.

```shell
gh stack add [flags] [branch]
```

Creates a new branch at the current HEAD, adds it to the top of the stack, and checks it out. You must run this command while on the topmost branch of a stack. If you do not provide a branch name, the command prompts for one.

You can optionally stage changes and create a commit as part of the `add` flow. When you provide `-m` without an explicit branch name, the branch name is generated automatically in date and slug format, such as `03-24-add_login`.

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-A, --all` | Stage all changes, including untracked files. Requires `-m`. |
| `-u, --update` | Stage changes to tracked files only. Requires `-m`. |
| `-m, --message <string>` | Create a commit with this message before creating the branch |

Note

`-A` and `-u` are mutually exclusive.

**Examples:**

```shell
# Create a branch by name
gh stack add api-routes

# Prompt for a branch name interactively
gh stack add

# Stage all changes, commit, and auto-generate the branch name
gh stack add -Am "Add login endpoint"

# Stage only tracked files, commit, and auto-generate the branch name
gh stack add -um "Fix auth bug"

# Commit already-staged changes and auto-generate the branch name
gh stack add -m "Add user model"

# Stage all changes, commit, and use an explicit branch name
gh stack add -Am "Add tests" test-layer

# Stage only tracked files, commit, and use an explicit branch name
gh stack add -um "Update docs" docs-layer
```

### [`gh stack view`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-view)

View the current stack.

```shell
gh stack view [flags]
```

Shows all branches in the stack, their ordering, pull request links, and the most recent commit with a relative timestamp. Output is piped through a pager, which respects `GIT_PAGER` or `PAGER`, and defaults to `less -R`.

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-s, --short` | Compact output (branch names only) |
| `--json` | Output stack data as JSON |

**Examples:**

```shell
gh stack view
gh stack view --short
gh stack view --json
```

### [`gh stack checkout`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-checkout)

Check out a stack by its stack number, a pull request number, a pull request URL, or a branch name.

```shell
gh stack checkout [<stack-number> | <pr-number> | <pr-url> | <branch>]
```

A bare number is interpreted first as a stack or pull request number. These are repository-scoped identifiers shown in the GitHub UI. If nothing matches the number, it is tried as a branch name.

When you reference a remote stack, the command fetches the stack on GitHub, pulls the branches, and sets up the stack locally. If the stack already exists locally and matches, the command switches to the branch. If the local and remote stacks have different compositions, you are prompted to resolve the conflict.

When you provide a branch name, the command resolves it against locally tracked stacks only.

When you run the command without arguments in an interactive terminal, it opens a searchable picker listing every stack available to you, both the stacks tracked locally and the stacks that exist only on GitHub. Each row shows the stack number, its bottom and top branch, base branch, a status bar summarizing how many of its pull requests are merged, open, closed, or not yet pushed, and whether the stack is available locally or only on the remote. Filter with the **All**, **Local**, and **Remote** tabs, or type `/` to search. Fully merged stacks are omitted. Selecting a remote-only stack clones it locally before switching to it.

**Examples:**

```shell
# Check out a stack by its stack number
gh stack checkout 7

# Check out a stack by pull request number
gh stack checkout 42

# Check out a stack by pull request URL
gh stack checkout https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/42

# Check out a stack by branch name (local only)
gh stack checkout feature-auth

# Interactive — pick from all available stacks (local and remote)
gh stack checkout
```

### [`gh stack modify`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-modify)

Interactively restructure the current stack.

```shell
gh stack modify [flags]
```

Opens an interactive terminal UI for restructuring a stack. All changes are staged in the interface and applied together when you press `Ctrl` + `S`. You cannot modify branches from merged pull requests.

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--continue` | Continue after resolving conflicts |
| `--abort` | Abort the modify session and restore the stack to its state before you ran the command |

**Preconditions**

The command checks these conditions before opening the interface:

1. You must have an active stack checked out locally.
2. Your working tree must be clean, with no uncommitted changes.
3. No rebase is in progress.
4. No pull request in the stack is queued for merge.
5. Commit history must be linear, with no merge commits and no diverged branches.

**Operations**

| Operation | Key | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drop | `x` | Remove branch and its commits from the stack. The local branch and associated pull request are preserved. |
| Fold down | `d` | Absorb commits into the branch below, toward the trunk. The folded branch is removed from the stack. |
| Fold up | `u` | Absorb commits into the branch above, away from the trunk. The folded branch is removed from the stack. |
| Insert below | `i` | Insert a new empty branch below the cursor, toward the trunk. |
| Insert above | `I` | Insert a new empty branch above the cursor, away from the trunk. |
| Move down | `Shift` + `↓` | Reorder the branch down, toward the trunk. |
| Move up | `Shift` + `↑` | Reorder the branch up, away from the trunk. |
| Rename | `r` | Rename the branch, using an inline prompt. |
| Undo | `z` | Undo the last staged action. |

**Apply phase**

When you press `Ctrl` + `S`, the staged changes are applied by renaming branches, inserting new branches, folding or dropping branches, and running a cascading rebase to create a linear commit history with the stack state you want.

If a rebase conflict occurs, you can either:

- Resolve the conflicts, stage the files, then run `gh stack modify --continue`.
- Run `gh stack modify --abort` to abort the operation and restore the stack to its previous state.

**After modifying**

If you have already created a stack of pull requests on GitHub, run `gh stack submit` to push the updated branches and recreate the stack. The old stack is replaced automatically.

**Examples:**

```shell
# Open the interactive modify interface
gh stack modify

# Continue after resolving a conflict
gh stack modify --continue

# Abort and restore to the previous state
gh stack modify --abort
```

### [`gh stack unstack`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-unstack)

Remove a stack from local tracking and unstack it on GitHub. This command is also available as `gh stack delete`.

```shell
gh stack unstack [<stack-number>] [flags]
```

With no argument, the command targets the active stack, which is the stack that contains the currently checked out branch. It unstacks the stack on GitHub and removes local tracking.

Provide a stack number, the identifier shown in the stack UI on GitHub, to unstack a specific stack. This works from anywhere in the repository, whether or not the stack is checked out locally, because the stack is unstacked directly through the GitHub API. When the stack is also available locally, its local tracking is removed as well.

Pull requests that are merged, merging, or queued for merge cannot be removed from a stack on GitHub and remain part of the stack. When every pull request is removed, the stack is dissolved and any local tracking is removed. When some pull requests remain stacked, the stack is kept and local tracking, if any, is unchanged. Use `--local` to skip the remote operation and only remove local tracking.

This command is useful when you need to restructure a stack by removing a branch, inserting a branch, reordering branches, renaming branches, or making other large changes. After unstacking, use `gh stack init` to recreate the stack with the structure you want. Existing branches are adopted automatically.

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--local` | Only remove the stack locally, keeping it on GitHub |

**Examples:**

```shell
# Unstack the current stack on GitHub and remove local tracking
gh stack unstack

# Unstack a specific stack by its number
gh stack unstack 7

# Only remove local tracking
gh stack unstack --local
```

## [Remote operations](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#remote-operations)

### [`gh stack submit`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-submit)

Push all branches, then create or update pull requests and the stack on GitHub.

```shell
gh stack submit [flags]
```

Creates a pull request for every branch in the stack, pushing branches to the remote. After creating pull requests, `submit` automatically creates a stack on GitHub to link the pull requests together. If the stack already exists on GitHub, for example from a previous submit, new pull requests are added to the existing stack.

If every pull request in the stack has already been merged, that stack is complete and cannot be extended. In that case, `submit` automatically starts a new stack rooted at the trunk for your unmerged branches and creates it on GitHub, leaving the merged stack untouched.

In an interactive terminal, `submit` opens a full-screen editor on a single screen.

- **Left panel.** Every branch without a pull request is included by default. Deselect any you do not want to submit with `Ctrl` + `X`. Because each pull request builds on the branch below it, deselecting a branch also deselects the ones stacked above it, and re-including a branch re-includes the ones below it that it depends on. Branches that already have a pull request, whether open, draft, queued, or merged, are shown for context but are locked. Edit those on the web.
- **Right panel.** For the focused branch, draft the title and description, and choose whether the pull request opens ready for review or as a draft. The description is pre-filled from your repository's pull request template or commits, with a markdown preview and an `$EDITOR` escape. Focusing a locked branch shows a read-only card with a link to its pull request. Press `o` to open it in the browser.

Press `Ctrl` + `S` to submit all included pull requests at once. The editor supports both keyboard and mouse input. Pass `--auto`, or run the command in a non-interactive terminal such as CI, to skip the editor and use automatically generated titles.

If the branches already have open pull requests but no stack exists on GitHub, you have the option to link the pull requests into a stack with `Ctrl` + `B`.

In the editor, new pull requests default to ready for review. You can flip any pull request to draft with the toggle. With `--auto`, new pull requests are created as drafts unless you pass `--open`.

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--auto` | Skip the editor and use automatically generated pull request titles |
| `--open` | Create new pull requests as ready for review instead of drafts, and mark existing pull requests as ready for review |
| `--remote <name>` | Remote to push to (defaults to the automatically detected remote) |

**Examples:**

```shell
gh stack submit
gh stack submit --auto
gh stack submit --open
```

### [`gh stack sync`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-sync)

Fetch, rebase, push, and sync pull request state in a single command.

```shell
gh stack sync [flags]
```

Synchronizes the entire stack.

1. **Fetch.** Fetches the latest changes from `origin`.
2. **Reconcile the remote stack.** Mirrors the stack on GitHub locally. When pull requests have been added to the stack on GitHub, so that the remote is ahead of your local stack, their branches are pulled down and appended to your local stack automatically. When the local and remote stacks have genuinely diverged, for example because you added a branch locally while different pull requests were added to the stack on GitHub, you are prompted to resolve the difference. See [Diverged stacks](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands#diverged-stacks). In a non-interactive terminal, a divergence aborts the sync, and nothing is pushed or updated.
3. **Fast-forward trunk.** Fast-forwards the trunk branch to match the remote. This step is skipped if the branches have diverged.
4. **Cascade rebase.** Rebases all stack branches onto their updated parents, but only if trunk moved. If a conflict is detected, all branches are restored to their original state, and you are advised to run `gh stack rebase` to resolve conflicts interactively.
5. **Push.** Pushes all branches, using `--force-with-lease` if a rebase occurred.
6. **Sync pull requests.** Syncs pull request state from GitHub and reports the status of each pull request.
7. **Sync the stack.** Links the stack's open pull requests into a stack on GitHub, creating the remote stack object if it does not exist yet, or updating it if it is partially formed. This only happens when two or more pull requests exist. Sync never opens pull requests. Use `gh stack submit` for that.
8. **Prune.** In interactive terminals, prompts you to delete local branches for merged pull requests. Use `--prune` to prune automatically.

A clean remote-ahead update, where pull requests are added on top of your local stack, is pulled down automatically without prompting, so `sync` is safe to run in automation. Sync only prompts when the stacks have truly diverged.

#### [Diverged stacks](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#diverged-stacks)

When neither stack is a clean prefix of the other, for example because you added a branch locally while separate pull requests were added to the same stack on GitHub, sync cannot merge the two automatically. In an interactive terminal, it offers three choices.

- **Use the remote stack as the source of truth.** Replaces your local stack composition with the remote's, pulling any missing branches. If you were on a branch that the remote stack no longer contains, you are moved to the nearest surviving branch. This requires a clean working state with no uncommitted changes.
- **Delete the stack on GitHub.** Deletes the stack object on GitHub and stops the sync. Your pull requests and local branches are untouched, and only the stack on GitHub is removed. Recreate the stack with `gh stack submit`, running `gh stack modify` first if you want to change its structure. This is the way to make GitHub match your local stack, because `submit`, unlike `sync`, also creates pull requests for any branches you have not submitted yet.
- **Cancel.** Aborts the sync without pushing branches or updating any pull requests.

In a non-interactive terminal, a divergence aborts the sync, exiting successfully, without pushing branches or updating pull requests. Resolve it by unstacking and recreating the stack.

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--remote <name>` | Remote to fetch from and push to (defaults to the automatically detected remote) |
| `--prune` | Delete local branches for merged pull requests |

**Examples:**

```shell
gh stack sync

# Sync and automatically prune merged branches
gh stack sync --prune
```

### [`gh stack rebase`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-rebase)

Pull from the remote and run a cascading rebase across the stack.

```shell
gh stack rebase [flags] [branch]
```

Fetches the latest changes from `origin`, then ensures each branch in the stack has the tip of the previous layer in its commit history. Branches are rebased in order, from the trunk upward.

If a branch's pull request has been merged, the rebase automatically switches to `--onto` mode to correctly replay commits on top of the merge target.

If a rebase conflict occurs, the operation pauses and prints the conflicted files with line numbers. Resolve the conflicts, stage them with `git add`, then continue with `--continue`. To undo the entire rebase, use `--abort` to restore all branches to their state before the rebase.

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--downstack` | Only rebase branches from the trunk to the current branch |
| `--upstack` | Only rebase branches from the current branch to the top |
| `--no-trunk` | Skip the trunk. Only rebase stack branches onto each other, with no fetch and no trunk rebase. |
| `--continue` | Continue the rebase after resolving conflicts |
| `--abort` | Abort the rebase and restore all branches to their state before the rebase |
| `--remote <name>` | Remote to fetch from (defaults to the automatically detected remote) |
| `--committer-date-is-author-date` | Set the committer date to the author date during the rebase. Alias: `--preserve-dates`. |

| Argument | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `[branch]` | Target branch (defaults to the current branch) |

**Examples:**

```shell
# Rebase the entire stack
gh stack rebase

# Only rebase branches below the current one
gh stack rebase --downstack

# Only rebase branches above the current one
gh stack rebase --upstack

# Rebase stack branches without pulling from or rebasing with trunk
gh stack rebase --no-trunk

# After resolving a conflict
gh stack rebase --continue

# Abort rebase and restore everything
gh stack rebase --abort

# Rebase and preserve committer date as author date
gh stack rebase --committer-date-is-author-date
```

### [`gh stack push`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-push)

Push the active branches in the current stack to the remote.

```shell
gh stack push [flags]
```

Pushes every active branch, excluding merged and queued branches, in a single `git push`, using an explicit per-branch `--force-with-lease` check. The update is not atomic. Branches whose leases pass can be updated even if another branch is rejected. Fix the rejected branch and run the command again. Branches that were already updated remain unchanged. This command does not create or update pull requests. Use `gh stack submit` for that.

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--remote <name>` | Remote to push to (defaults to the automatically detected remote) |

**Examples:**

```shell
gh stack push
gh stack push --remote upstream
```

### [`gh stack link`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-link)

Link pull requests into a stack on GitHub without local tracking.

```shell
gh stack link [flags] <stack-number | branch-or-pr> <branch-or-pr> [...]
```

Creates or updates a stack on GitHub from branch names or pull request numbers and URLs. This command does not create or modify any local tracking state. It is designed for people who manage branches with other tools locally, such as Jujutsu, Sapling, or git-town, and want to open a stack of pull requests. See [Use other tools with stacked pull requests](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/use-other-tools-with-stacked-pull-requests).

You provide arguments in stack order, from bottom to top. Branch arguments are pushed to the remote automatically before pull requests are created or looked up. For branches that already have open pull requests, those pull requests are used. For branches without pull requests, new pull requests are created automatically with the correct base branch chaining. Existing pull requests whose base branch does not match the expected chain are corrected automatically.

If the pull requests are not yet in a stack, a new stack is created. If some of the pull requests are already in a stack, the existing stack is updated to include the new pull requests. Existing pull requests are never removed from a stack, because the update is additive only.

To grow an existing stack without listing its pull requests again, pass a stack number, the number shown in the stack UI on GitHub, as the first argument. The remaining arguments are appended to the top of that stack. Arguments already in the stack are skipped, and arguments that belong to a different stack are rejected. Because stack and pull request numbers never overlap, a numeric first argument is treated as a stack only when it matches an existing stack. Otherwise it is treated as a pull request or branch.

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--base <branch>` | Base branch for the bottom of the stack (defaults to the repository's default branch). This flag is ignored when you add to an existing stack. |
| `--open` | Mark new and existing pull requests as ready for review |
| `--remote <name>` | Remote to push to (defaults to the automatically detected remote) |

**Examples:**

```shell
# Link branches into a stack (pushes, creates pull requests, creates stack)
gh stack link feature-auth feature-api feature-ui

# Link existing pull requests by number
gh stack link 10 20 30

# Link existing pull requests by URL
gh stack link https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/10 https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/20

# Add branches to an existing stack of pull requests
gh stack link 42 43 feature-auth feature-ui

# Append to the top of an existing stack by its stack number, with no need
# to list the pull requests already in stack 7 again
gh stack link 7 48 feature-ui

# Use a different base branch and mark pull requests as ready for review
gh stack link --base develop --open feat-a feat-b feat-c
```

### [`gh stack merge`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-merge)

Merge one or more stacked pull requests at once.

```shell
gh stack merge [<stack-number> | <pr-number>]
```

Merges every pull request in the stack, up to and including the pull request you choose, into the base branch. The merge is a single, all-or-nothing operation. If any pull request cannot be merged, none of them are merged.

With no argument, the command uses the active local stack. Provide a stack number to merge a stack that you do not have checked out, which is a purely remote operation, or provide a pull request number to merge directly up to that pull request.

In an interactive terminal, the command prompts you to choose which pull requests to merge, pick the merge method, and confirm. In a non-interactive terminal, or when you use `--yes`, the whole stack, or everything up to the pull request you specify, is merged without prompting, using the merge method you last used unless you specify one.

Only basic pull request state is checked before merging. Each pull request must be open and must not be a draft. GitHub evaluates branch protection and repository rules when the merge runs, and any failure is reported back to you.

Note

You cannot bypass merge requirements when you merge stacked pull requests.

If the base branch uses a merge queue, the stack is added to the queue instead of being merged directly. The queue chooses the merge method, so the prompt skips the merge method step, and the `--merge-method`, `--squash`, `--rebase`, and `--merge` flags are ignored with a warning. The pull requests you select are added to the queue together, but they merge as the queue processes them, so they can land in separate groups rather than all at once.

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--merge-method <method>` | Merge method to use: `merge`, `squash`, or `rebase` |
| `--merge`, `--squash`, `--rebase` | Shorthands for the corresponding merge method |
| `-y, --yes` | Merge without prompting for confirmation |

**Examples:**

```shell
# Merge the current stack, choosing pull requests interactively
gh stack merge

# Merge a stack you do not have checked out, by stack number
gh stack merge 7

# Merge everything up to and including pull request 42
gh stack merge 42

# Merge the whole current stack without prompting, squashing commits
gh stack merge --yes --squash
```

## [Navigation](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#navigation)

Navigation commands move you between branches in the current stack without having to remember branch names. The bottom of the stack is the branch closest to the trunk, and the top is the branch furthest from it. `up` moves away from the trunk, and `down` moves toward it.

All navigation commands clamp to the bounds of the stack. Moving up from the top, or down from the bottom, does nothing and displays a message.

### [`gh stack switch`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-switch)

Interactively switch to another branch in the stack.

```shell
gh stack switch
```

Shows an interactive picker listing all branches in the current stack, ordered from top, furthest from the trunk, to bottom, closest to the trunk, with their position number. Select a branch to check it out.

This command requires an interactive terminal.

**Examples:**

```shell
gh stack switch
#    → Select a branch in the stack to switch to
#      5. frontend
#      4. api-endpoints
#      3. auth-layer
#      2. db-schema
#      1. config-setup
```

### [`gh stack up`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-up)

Move up toward the top of the stack, away from the trunk.

```shell
gh stack up [n]
```

Moves up `n` branches, defaulting to 1. If you are on the trunk branch, `up` moves to the first stack branch.

**Examples:**

```shell
# Move up one layer
gh stack up

# Move up three layers
gh stack up 3
```

### [`gh stack down`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-down)

Move down toward the bottom of the stack, toward the trunk.

```shell
gh stack down [n]
```

Moves down `n` branches, defaulting to 1.

**Examples:**

```shell
# Move down one layer
gh stack down

# Move down two layers
gh stack down 2
```

### [`gh stack top`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-top)

Jump to the top of the stack.

```shell
gh stack top
```

Checks out the branch furthest from the trunk.

### [`gh stack bottom`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-bottom)

Jump to the bottom of the stack.

```shell
gh stack bottom
```

Checks out the branch closest to the trunk.

### [`gh stack trunk`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-trunk)

Jump to the trunk branch.

```shell
gh stack trunk
```

Checks out the trunk branch of the current stack, such as `main`. You must be on a branch that is part of a stack.

## [Utilities](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#utilities)

### [`gh stack alias`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-alias)

Create a short command alias so you can type less.

```shell
gh stack alias [flags] [name]
```

Installs a small wrapper script into `~/.local/bin/` that forwards all arguments to `gh stack`. The default alias name is `gs`, but you can choose any name by passing it as an argument. After setup, you can run `gs push` instead of `gh stack push`.

On Windows, automatic alias creation is not supported. The command prints manual instructions for creating a batch file or PowerShell function.

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--remove` | Remove an alias you created previously |

**Examples:**

```shell
# Create the default alias (gs), so that "gs push" and "gs view" both work
gh stack alias

# Create a custom alias
gh stack alias gst

# Remove an alias
gh stack alias --remove
gh stack alias --remove gst
```

### [`gh stack feedback`](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#gh-stack-feedback)

Share feedback about the `gh stack` extension.

```shell
gh stack feedback [title]
```

Opens a discussion in the [gh-stack repository](https://github.com/github/gh-stack) so you can submit feedback. You can optionally provide a title for the discussion post.

**Examples:**

```shell
gh stack feedback
gh stack feedback "Support for reordering branches"
```

## [Environment variables](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#environment-variables)

| Variable | Values | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GH_STACK_THEME` | `auto` (default), `light`, `dark` | Controls the color palette of the interactive screens for `submit`, `modify`, and `view`, and all colored command output. Colors adapt to your terminal background automatically. Set this variable to force the light or dark palette when a terminal does not report its background, which can happen in some SSH or `tmux` setups. |

```shell
# Force the light palette for one command
GH_STACK_THEME=light gh stack view
```

## [Exit codes](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-prs-cli-commands\#exit-codes)

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Success |
| 1 | Generic error |
| 2 | Not in a stack, or stack not found |
| 3 | Rebase conflict |
| 4 | GitHub API failure |
| 5 | Invalid arguments or flags |
| 6 | Disambiguation required, because the branch belongs to multiple stacks |
| 7 | Rebase already in progress |
| 8 | Stack is locked by another process |
| 9 | Stacked pull requests are not enabled for this repository |
| 10 | Modify session interrupted, and recovery is required |
